issues.legal_issue: A tenant transferred to another town loses protection from eviction that depended on the tenant's employment in an essential service.
material_facts: The tenant worked in a service notified as essential and was protected from eviction on that basis.
The tenant was transferred from the town where the rented premises were located to another town.
The landlord sought eviction under the rent-control law, and the High Court held that the tenant remained protected despite the transfer.
issues.conclusion: The tenant's transfer to another town ended the protection against eviction under Section 10(4)(i).
issues.legal_principle: Section 10(4)(i) of the Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960 bars eviction under Section 10(3) for tenants engaged in government-notified essential services. Read in light of the provision's purpose—to avoid hardship that could interfere with the provision of essential services—the protection ceases when the tenant is transferred to another town and is no longer required to provide those services at the original place. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: A landlord sought eviction of a tenant under a rent-control law.
predicates.tenant_in_notified_essential_service: The tenant worked in a service that the government had notified as essential.
predicates.tenant_transferred_to_another_town: The tenant's employer transferred the tenant from the town where the rented premises were located to another town.

issues.definition: When a rent-control eviction proceeding concerns a tenant protected because of essential-service employment, a transfer to another town means that the protection ceases.

issues.legal_issue: A revisional court may not reassess evidence and overturn concurrent factual findings when no legal infirmity in those findings is shown.
material_facts: The Rent Controller and the first appellate authority both found that the landlord's need for the premises was bona fide.
The High Court reassessed the evidence in revision and reversed the concurrent findings.
No legal infirmity in the concurrent findings was shown.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was not entitled to reassess the evidence and reverse the concurrent findings in revision.
issues.legal_principle: In exercising revisional jurisdiction, the High Court may not reassess evidence to displace concurrent factual findings when no legal infirmity in those findings has been shown. No earlier cases were relied on.

rule.if: rent_control_revision and concurrent_factual_findings and revisional_court_reassessed_evidence and no_legal_infirmity_shown

predicates.rent_control_revision: A tenant challenged an eviction decision through revision in a rent-control proceeding.
predicates.concurrent_factual_findings: The initial decision-maker and the first appellate authority reached the same factual finding.
predicates.revisional_court_reassessed_evidence: The revisional court reconsidered the evidence and reached a different factual finding.
predicates.no_legal_infirmity_shown: No legal defect in the concurrent findings was identified.

issues.definition: In a rent-control revision, reassessing evidence to overturn concurrent factual findings is impermissible when no legal defect in those findings is shown.
